title: Mirabel and the Will
premise: Estate lawyer Ansel Sterling is summoned to the decaying seaside town of Greywater to read the will of Edith Marlowe, a woman she never met — only to discover the will names Ansel herself as executor and heir, along with a confession letter postmarked the day after Edith's funeral. The letter admits to a drowning thirty years ago, but the details don't match any death on record. As Ansel digs through Edith's papers, she uncovers a web of swapped identities, forged alibis, and a found family of outsiders Edith sheltered for decades — one of whom knows exactly what happened at the tide pools in 1994. When the tide finally gives up what it took, Ansel learns the confession was written to protect her: Edith was her grandmother, and the 'drowning' was an accident Edith covered up to save a frightened teenager who grew up to become the only family Ansel has left. The killer was never a killer at all; the real crime was thirty years of silence, and the ending sees Ansel choosing to break it.
about_author: Jude Ashgrove is the pen name of a former probate clerk who spent a decade watching families unravel over paper. They write mysteries from a rented cottage on the northern coast, where the tide sets their writing schedule.

chapters.title: The Will That Shouldn't Exist
chapters.summary: Ansel Sterling's POV. A routine probate docket contains an anomaly: a will filed by Edith Marlowe naming Ansel — a stranger — as executor and sole heir alongside an unnamed beneficiary. Her firm's records show no connection. The emotional beat is professional unease curdling into personal compulsion as she books a train to Greywater against her partner's advice.

chapters.title: Greywater
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. She arrives in the salt-bleached town and finds Marlowe House shuttered but not empty — fresh flowers on the hall table, a kettle still warm. Neighbors watch her from doorways. The beat is creeping wrongness: someone expected her, and someone else has been living in the dead woman's house.

chapters.title: The Reading
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. In Edith's parlor, before a handful of wary locals, Ansel reads the will aloud. It bequeaths the house to her, a sealed envelope to 'the child of the tide,' and one condition: the estate passes only if she stays thirty days. The beat is public hostility masking private fear — everyone in the room knew Edith better than Ansel did.

chapters.title: Postmarked the Day After
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. She opens the confession letter: Edith admits to a drowning at the tide pools in 1994, a body that matches no missing-persons record. The letter ends mid-sentence. The emotional beat is vertigo — Ansel realizes the document is legally damning and deliberately incomplete, a hook meant to reel her in.

chapters.title: The Child of the Tide
chapters.summary: Alternating POV introducing Wren Calloway, a reclusive boat restorer who received an identical envelope. Wren burns hers unread. The beat is parallel dread: two strangers bound by a dead woman's design, each hiding a reason not to look too closely at 1994.

chapters.title: Alibis, Thirty Years Old
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Digging through Edith's files, Ansel finds meticulously preserved alibis for five townspeople dated to the week of the drowning — typed, notarized, too perfect. The beat is the lawyer's instinct firing: nobody builds alibis in advance unless they know a body will surface.

chapters.title: What the Tide Took
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren remembers 1994 in fragments: a storm, a scream, Edith's hands pulling her from the water. She visits the tide pools at low tide and finds a rusted locket wedged in the rocks. The beat is grief surfacing like a body — memory returning whether she wants it or not.

chapters.title: Five Names
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. She interviews the five alibied townspeople: the pub landlord, the retired doctor, the schoolteacher, the harbormaster, and Edith's gardener. Each account is smooth, rehearsed, identical in its gaps. The beat is quiet menace — the town isn't hiding one secret, it's maintaining one collectively.

chapters.title: The Room Behind the Bookcase
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Following drafts and dust lines, Ansel finds a hidden room in Marlowe House: children's drawings, a boy's clothing, thirty years of birthday cards signed 'Edie.' Someone lived here. The beat is tenderness inside dread — Edith wasn't just hiding a crime, she was raising someone.

chapters.title: Missing Persons, 1994
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Records searches reveal a boy, Daniel Voss, reported missing that summer by a mother who withdrew the report three weeks later and left town. No body, no closure. The beat is cold horror: either Daniel drowned and was erased, or he never drowned at all.

chapters.title: Wren Breaks the Seal
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Haunted by the locket, Wren finally reads her envelope: Edith writes directly to her — 'You were the child of the tide, and I was your witness' — and asks forgiveness for a lie told to keep her safe. The beat is shattering recognition: Wren was there in 1994, and she was a child.

chapters.title: Convergence
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Ansel and Wren, each following the other's trail, collide at the tide pools in a storm. Distrust flares — each suspects the other of being the unnamed beneficiary with something to hide. The beat is two locked boxes forced open by weather and circumstance.

chapters.title: The Gardener's Hands
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. The gardener, Silas, nearly confesses, then warns her off: 'Edith buried it deep so it would stay buried. You're digging up more than bones.' That night his shed burns. The beat is escalation — the town's silence has teeth, and Ansel is now a target.

chapters.title: The Doctor's Second Signature
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Ansel discovers the 1994 death certificate bearing the doctor's signature — filed for a body that officially never existed. Confronted, the old man weeps: he certified a death Edith begged him to certify, to close a case that would have destroyed a child. The beat is moral inversion: the cover-up was mercy, or so he believes.

chapters.title: Daniel
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren pieces together the truth she's outrun for thirty years: Daniel Voss didn't drown — he survived, was hidden in Marlowe House, and grew up as Edith's ward. The birthday cards were his. The beat is devastating relief and betrayal braided together: the found family was real, and it excluded her.

chapters.title: Where Is He Now
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. If Daniel lived, where did he go? Estate records show annual payments to an offshore account until five years ago, then nothing. Ansel traces the account's final transfer — to a hospice in the next county. The beat is racing hope shadowed by the obvious question the chapter refuses to answer yet.

chapters.title: The Hospice Visitor Log
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. At the hospice, Ansel finds Daniel Voss died four years ago — and that his last visitor, every week for a year, signed in as E. Marlowe. Beside his bed they kept a shoebox: photographs, the locket's twin, and a letter addressed to 'the lawyer, when she comes.' The beat is awe at Edith's long game — she planned this inheritance across decades.

chapters.title: The Second Confession
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Daniel's letter tells the truth at last: in 1994, fourteen-year-old Wren pushed Daniel during a quarrel at the pools; he struck his head; Edith, arriving after, staged the drowning to protect both children. The alibis, the certificate, the silence — all of it built around a traumatized girl. The beat is the mystery collapsing into tragedy: there was no murderer, only fear multiplied by thirty years.

chapters.title: What We Owe the Dead
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Ansel brings the truth to Wren, who already half-knew and has been drowning in guilt since childhood. The confrontation is raw — rage, denial, then collapse. The beat is the novel's emotional climax: Wren must decide whether thirty years of Edith's protection was love or theft of her own life.

chapters.title: The Beneficiary
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. The will's condition resolves: the 'child of the tide' clause names Wren, making her co-heir — Edith's final act was forcing the two women together. But Silas, desperate to end the digging, confronts them at Marlowe House with fire again in hand. The beat is danger made intimate: the last guardian of the secret would rather burn it than speak it.

chapters.title: High Water
chapters.summary: Climax, dual POV. At the tide pools, with the spring tide rising, Silas breaks down: he was Daniel's father, and Edith stole his son to punish him for the boy's neglect. The truth of 1994 stands, but the human wreckage is laid bare. The beat is catharsis at the waterline — confessions exchanged as the sea takes back the shore.

chapters.title: Probate
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV, epilogue. Ansel settles the estate honestly: the false certificate reported, Wren's name cleared under juvenile confidentiality, Marlowe House deeded jointly. She stays past the thirty days. The final image is the two women planting Edith's garden as the tide turns. The beat is resolution as choice — inheritance isn't what you're given, it's what you agree to carry.
